items.title: Records compare by value
items.body:
Each question here names a Goal, then asks which observation or code shape shows you reached it. The right choice is the one the chapter's own example demonstrates.

A `record` is a class, but the compiler generates **value-based equality** for it. `==` compares every property, so two separately built `Person("Sam", "Lee", 30)` values are equal and the program prints True. The chapter's example says exactly that and contrasts it with a normal class, where `==` would compare references.

Why the others are wrong:
- **True only after string.Intern**: interning is about strings and is not involved; the generated equality compares the properties' values.
- **False, == compares references for any class**: that is true for ordinary classes, but records override it.
- **does not compile, needs Equals()**: records support `==` directly; the example uses it.

excerpts.quote: var p2 = new Person("Sam", "Lee", 30); Console.WriteLine(p1 == p2);              // True! Value equality — compares all properties
Compare to a class, where `==` would be reference equality

items.title: AsNoTracking for read-only queries
items.body:
Each question here names a Goal, then asks which observation or code shape shows you reached it. The right choice is the one the chapter's own example demonstrates.

By default EF Core tracks every entity it returns so that it can detect changes and save them later. A read-only GET endpoint never saves, so that tracking is wasted work and memory. Adding `.AsNoTracking()` turns it off for that query. The chapter recommends exactly this for GET endpoints and reports.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Include every navigation**: that loads more data, making the query heavier, not lighter.
- **foreach over the DbSet**: that still runs a tracked query, and loses the async `ToListAsync` call.
- **SaveChanges after the query**: there is nothing to save; it does not remove tracked entities.

excerpts.quote: For read-only queries (you won't modify and save), disable tracking — it's faster and uses less memory:
Use `AsNoTracking()` for GET endpoints and reports.

items.title: Start both tasks, then await WhenAll
items.body:
Each question here names a Goal, then asks which observation or code shape shows you reached it. The right choice is the one the chapter's own example demonstrates.

An async method starts working as soon as you call it. If you `await` the first call before making the second, the second does not even start until the first finishes, so the total is about the **sum**. If you call both first (keeping the tasks), and then `await Task.WhenAll(taskA, taskB)`, they overlap and the total is about the **slower** one. After `WhenAll`, reading `.Result` is safe because both have completed.

Why the others are wrong:
- **shared DbContext in Parallel.ForEach**: the chapter warns EF Core contexts are not thread-safe, and these are HTTP calls anyway.
- **two sequential awaits**: the chapter labels this the slow, sequential version.
- **Task.WhenAny**: it completes when the **first** task finishes, so the second may not be done when you read it.

excerpts.quote: // Concurrent — total time ≈ the slower of the two (fast): Task<User> taskA = GetUserAsync(1);    // start (don't await yet) Task<User> taskB = GetUserAsync(2);    // start await Task.WhenAll(taskA, taskB);      // wait for both
`Task.WhenAny` completes when the first task finishes (useful for timeouts/races).

items.title: A deferred query sees the list as it is when enumerated
items.body:
Each question here names a Goal, then asks which observation or code shape shows you reached it. The right choice is the one the chapter's own example demonstrates.

`Where` does not filter anything when you call it. It returns a query that filters later, when you enumerate it. By the time the `foreach` runs, `source` contains 1, 2, 3 and 4, so the filter sees all four and the loop writes 2 then 4. This is the chapter's own example, with the comment "prints 2 4 — sees the added 4!".

Why the others are wrong:
- **InvalidOperationException**: that error is for changing a collection while you are enumerating it; here the `Add` happens before enumeration starts.
- **only 2, a snapshot**: `Where` keeps a reference to the list, not a copy.
- **nothing until ToList()**: a `foreach` enumerates the query just as `ToList()` does.

excerpts.quote: A deferred query reflects the *current* state of the source when enumerated, not when defined.
source.Add(4); foreach (var n in evens) Console.Write(n);    // prints 2 4 — sees the added 4!

items.title: with makes a modified copy
items.body:
Each question here names a Goal, then asks which observation or code shape shows you reached it. The right choice is the one the chapter's own example demonstrates.

`p1 with { Age = 31 }` creates a **new** record that copies every property of `p1` and changes `Age`. `p1` itself is not touched. So `older.Age` is 31 and `p1.Age` is still 30. The chapter calls this a non-destructive copy, and it is how you "change" a record whose positional properties are init-only.

Why the others are wrong:
- **same reference, p1 == older**: `with` builds a new object, and since `Age` differs, value equality would say false anyway.
- **compile error**: init-only properties cannot be set after construction, but `with` is allowed to set them on the new copy; that is its purpose.
- **both are 31**: the original is unchanged; the example prints "still 30".

excerpts.quote: // Non-destructive copy with 'with' (creates a modified copy, original unchanged): var older = p1 with { Age = 31 };
Console.WriteLine(p1.Age);                // still 30

items.title: The ! operator only silences the compiler
items.body:
Each question here names a Goal, then asks which observation or code shape shows you reached it. The right choice is the one the chapter's own example demonstrates.

`maybe!` tells the compiler "trust me, this is not null here", so it stops warning. That is all it does. The chapter is direct: `!` does not change runtime behaviour. If `maybe` really is null, `definitely` is null too, and reading `definitely.Length` throws a `NullReferenceException` when it runs.

Why the others are wrong:
- **substitutes an empty string**: nothing is substituted; that would be `?? ""`, a different operator.
- **throws ArgumentNullException at the assignment**: the assignment just copies the null; no check runs there.
- **compiler inserts a null check**: `!` removes a warning, it does not add code.

excerpts.quote: **`!` does not change runtime behavior** — it only silences the compiler. If you're wrong, you still get an NRE at runtime.
string definitely = maybe!;          // "trust me, it's not null"

items.title: A narrowing cast keeps the low 32 bits
items.body:
Each question here names a Goal, then asks which observation or code shape shows you reached it. The right choice is the one the chapter's own example demonstrates.

`(int)big` tells the compiler "I accept that this might lose data". In the default unchecked mode, the conversion simply keeps the lowest 32 bits of the 64-bit value and throws them into an `int`. For 5,000,000,000 that gives 705032704. There is no error and no warning at runtime, which is why the chapter shows it: casts can quietly give you a different number.

Why the others are wrong:
- **clamps to int.MaxValue**: C# casts do not clamp; they keep the low bits.
- **throws OverflowException**: that only happens in a `checked` context; the default is unchecked.
- **CS0220 compile error**: the value is in a variable, not a constant expression, so the compiler accepts the cast.

excerpts.quote: long big = 5_000_000_000L; int overflow = (int)big;   // 705032704 — keeps only the low 32 bits; no error (unchecked by default)
A cast says "I know this might lose data; do it anyway."

items.title: Without Include or lazy loading, Orders is just empty
items.body:
Each question here names a Goal, then asks which observation or code shape shows you reached it. The right choice is the one the chapter's own example demonstrates.

`ToListAsync()` loads the customers and nothing else. Lazy loading is **off** unless you install the proxies package and call `UseLazyLoadingProxies()`. So nothing ever loads `Orders`: each customer's collection is empty and the loop prints 0 for every one. The chapter calls this a silent wrong answer, which is worse than an error because nothing tells you.

Why the others are wrong:
- **N+1 queries**: that only happens with lazy loading switched on; the question says no proxies.
- **automatic join**: EF joins related data only when you ask with `Include` (or project it in a `Select`).
- **throws**: EF does not complain; the collection is simply not filled.

excerpts.quote: lazy loading is OFF unless you install Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Proxies and // call UseLazyLoadingProxies(). Without it, c.Orders is just empty and prints 0 — // a silent wrong answer.

items.title: async all the way down
items.body:
Each question here names a Goal, then asks which observation or code shape shows you reached it. The right choice is the one the chapter's own example demonstrates.

Blocking on a task with `.Result` or `.Wait()` can deadlock in some environments: the blocked thread is the very one the rest of the async method needs in order to finish. The chapter's rule is to make the caller `async` too and `await` the call: `var data = await FetchDataAsync();`. If you remember one rule from the chapter, it is this one.

Why the others are wrong:
- **.Wait() then .Result**: this is the blocking pattern the chapter says never to use.
- **Task.Run(...).Result**: it still blocks the calling thread with `.Result`, and the chapter says even when blocking does not deadlock it wastes a thread.
- **.Result is safe in modern .NET**: the chapter only allows `.Result` on a task you know has already completed.

excerpts.quote: **Never block on async code with `.Result` or `.Wait()`.**
**`async` all the way down; never `.Result`/`.Wait()`.**

items.title: Start here: the C# chapters this pack draws on
items.body:
This repo is a C# course from "I can write basic code" to mid-level backend work. The README's advice is simple: read in order, and type the code yourself. You learn C# by fighting the compiler.

This pack's reading steps and questions come from these chapters, so read them in this order:

1. `02-types-and-variables.md`: value vs reference types and conversions (casts).
2. `07-structs-records-enums.md`: structs, records, `with`, and `record struct`.
3. `10-linq.md`: LINQ operators, and the section on deferred execution.
4. `11-exceptions-and-resources.md`: try/catch, and what to do after you catch.
5. `13-async-await.md`: `Task.WhenAll` and the deadlock trap.
6. `15-nullable-reference-types.md`: `string?` and the `!` operator.
7. `19-entity-framework-core.md`: loading related data, tracking, and client vs server evaluation.

The code samples put the printed output in a comment on the same line (`// still 30`). Read those comments carefully; most of the questions are about exactly that output. Each chapter up to 18 also has an `-examples.md` companion with extra drills.

excerpts.quote: Read in order. Each chapter builds on the last. **Type the code yourself** — do not just read it.
Chapters 00–18 each have a companion `NN-topic-examples.md` file (20 worked snippets plus a table of 40 one-liners) for repetition; chapters 19–24 have no examples file.

readMore.why: The full table of contents and how the course is meant to be used.
How to work through the examples files in passes.

items.title: Bare throw keeps the original stack trace
items.body:
Each question here names a Goal, then asks which observation or code shape shows you reached it. The right choice is the one the chapter's own example demonstrates.

To log and then let the same exception keep travelling up, end the `catch` with a bare `throw;`. It re-throws the exception you caught and keeps its original stack trace, so whoever reads the error still sees where it really started. The chapter calls this a classic interview gotcha.

Why the others are wrong:
- **throw new Exception(ex.Message)**: that is a brand-new exception; the original type and stack trace are lost (at best you would pass `ex` as the inner exception).
- **throw ex;**: the chapter marks this WRONG: it resets the stack trace to the catch block.
- **return and a status flag**: the exception stops there; it does not continue up the stack at all.

excerpts.quote: throw;          // RE-THROW — preserves the original stack trace // throw ex;    // WRONG — resets the stack trace, hides where it really came from
**Use bare `throw;`**, never `throw ex;`.

items.title: Concept: what the compiler checks versus what runs
items.body:
A second idea runs through the type chapters: some C# features are **instructions to the compiler**, while others change what the running program does. Knowing which is which removes many surprises.

For each feature below, find the chapter's example, decide for yourself which side it is on, and then check the chapter's own words:

- an explicit cast such as `(int)` applied to a value that does not fit (chapter 02, the section on explicit conversions): what happens, and is an error raised at compile time, at runtime, or not at all?
- nullable annotations such as `string?` and the `!` operator (chapter 15): what exactly do they change, and when?
- records (chapter 07): which code the compiler generates for you, and how a positional `record` differs from a positional `record struct`.

The chapters state these things explicitly; look for the words "compile time" and "runtime", and for the output comments next to each example.

excerpts.quote: C# is **statically typed**: every variable has a type known at compile time, and the compiler stops you from misusing it.
# 15 — Nullable Reference Types
Compare to a class, where `==` would be reference equality, `ToString` would print the type name, and you'd hand-write `with`-style copies. Records eliminate all that boilerplate.

readMore.why: record struct, and when to use records versus classes.
The whole nullable chapter; short and practical.

items.title: string? is a compile-time signal
items.body:
Each question here names a Goal, then asks which observation or code shape shows you reached it. The right choice is the one the chapter's own example demonstrates.

With nullable reference types on, the compiler treats `string` as "should never be null" and `string?` as "may be null", and it warns you when the code does not match. That is analysis done while compiling. When the program runs, `string` and `string?` are the same type. The `?` signals intent to the compiler and to other readers.

Why the others are wrong:
- **turns off null checks**: it does the opposite: it asks the compiler to make you check before use.
- **assigning null throws at runtime**: the chapter shows assigning null to a non-nullable `string` gives a compiler **warning**, not a runtime error.
- **compiles to Nullable of string**: the `Nullable` wrapper is for value types such as `int?`; for reference types the `?` does not create a new runtime type.

excerpts.quote: It's a **compile-time analysis** — at runtime, `string` and `string?` are the same type.
name = null;               // ⚠️ compiler WARNING: assigning null to non-nullable

items.title: readonly record struct for an immutable value
items.body:
Each question here names a Goal, then asks which observation or code shape shows you reached it. The right choice is the one the chapter's own example demonstrates.

The chapter points out an asymmetry. A positional `record` (a class) gets init-only properties. A positional `record struct` gets ordinary **settable** properties, so `Point` is mutable. To get init-only properties on a value-type record, add `readonly`: `public readonly record struct Pixel(int X, int Y);`.

Why the others are wrong:
- **record struct already gets init-only**: this is the exact mistake the chapter warns about; its comment says "mutable!".
- **plain struct with public fields**: public fields can be assigned freely, and it is not a record.
- **sealed record struct**: this does not compile. A struct is already sealed, so `sealed` is not a valid modifier on a `record struct` (error CS0106). And `sealed` is about inheritance anyway, not about whether properties can be set.

excerpts.quote: public record struct Point(int X, int Y);          // X and Y are get; set; — mutable! public readonly record struct Pixel(int X, int Y); // X and Y are get; init; — immutable
a positional `record` (class) gets `init`-only properties, but a positional `record struct` gets ordinary **settable** properties.

items.title: Concept: when does the code actually run?
items.body:
Several chapters share one idea: **the line you write is not always the moment the work happens.** This reading tells you where to look; the chapters themselves give the answers.

- **LINQ.** The LINQ chapter has a section on deferred execution. Note exactly when a `Where` or `Select` does its work, and what data it sees at that moment. Then predict what changes if the source list is changed after the query is written, and run it.
- **async.** In the async chapter, compare the example that awaits calls one after another with the one that starts several tasks first. Work out the total time of each.
- **EF Core.** The EF chapter has a section on where a query "stops being SQL". Read what current EF Core does when a query contains a method it cannot translate, and when exactly the SQL is sent to the database.

When you read an example, ask: at which line does the real work happen, and what is the state of the data at that moment? Write your prediction down before you read the output comment.

excerpts.quote: **LINQ** (Language Integrated Query) is how you filter, transform, sort, group, and aggregate data in C#.
Asynchronous programming is **non-negotiable** for modern .NET backend work.
Know *where* your query stops being SQL and starts being C#.

readMore.why: The deferred-execution section with its worked example.

items.title: An untranslatable Where throws in modern EF Core
items.body:
Each question here names a Goal, then asks which observation or code shape shows you reached it. The right choice is the one the chapter's own example demonstrates.

EF Core turns your LINQ into SQL. A custom C# method like `MyComplexFormat(c)` has no SQL equivalent. Very old EF would quietly fetch everything and run it in memory; modern EF **throws** instead. There is one exception, the final `Select`, which EF may run on the client after fetching. A `Where` or `OrderBy` it cannot translate always throws. The fix the chapter shows: filter with translatable code, `ToListAsync()`, then call your method in memory.

Why the others are wrong:
- **silently filters in memory**: that was the behaviour before EF Core 3.0, which the chapter contrasts with today.
- **translates the method body to SQL**: EF cannot see inside an arbitrary C# method.
- **ignores the predicate**: EF never drops a filter silently; that would return wrong data.

excerpts.quote: If you call something it **can't** translate, older EF (before Core 3.0) would silently run it in memory (slow); modern EF **throws** instead.
but a `Where`/`OrderBy` it can't translate always throws.

items.title: The C# 14 Reverse gotcha on arrays
items.body:
Each question here names a Goal, then asks which observation or code shape shows you reached it. The right choice is the one the chapter's own example demonstrates.

In C# 14 / .NET 10, calling `nums.Reverse()` on an **array** no longer means LINQ's lazy `Enumerable.Reverse`. It binds to the span version, `MemoryExtensions.Reverse`, which reverses the array **in place** and returns nothing. To get a reversed sequence and leave the array alone, call the LINQ method explicitly as a static method: `Enumerable.Reverse(nums)`.

Why the others are wrong:
- **nums.Reverse().ToArray()**: `nums.Reverse()` now returns nothing, so there is nothing to call `ToArray()` on, and the array would already be reversed.
- **Array.Sort with a descending comparer**: that sorts, which is not reversing, and it modifies the array.
- **nums.Reverse() binds to LINQ**: that was true before; the gotcha is that it no longer does on arrays.

excerpts.quote: when `nums` is an **array**, `nums.Reverse()` now binds to `MemoryExtensions.Reverse(Span<T>)`, which reverses the array *in place* and returns nothing — not LINQ's lazy `Enumerable.Reverse`.
If you want a reversed sequence without touching the array, call `Enumerable.Reverse(nums)` explicitly.
